title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
summary: John is told to measure the temple and its worshipers but to leave the outer court to the nations, who will trample the holy city for 42 months. Two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days with the powers of Moses and Elijah, are killed by the beast from the Abyss, lie unburied for three and a half days, and are raised and taken up to heaven. The seventh trumpet then sounds, heaven announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and God's temple in heaven opens to show the ark of his covenant.
story: The interlude that began in chapter 10 continues. John has eaten the scroll and been told to prophesy; now he sees what prophetic witness looks like in a hostile world. The people of God are measured and protected in their worship yet exposed to trampling; their witnesses speak with power, are killed, and are vindicated by resurrection. Their story follows the shape of Jesus' own. Then the seventh trumpet, long delayed, sounds, and heaven sings the end of the story before the book tells it: God has begun to reign. Chapter 12 will step back to show the cosmic conflict behind everything the church has faced.
historical:
The imagery of a trampled city for 42 months draws on Daniel. Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 speak of a time, times, and half a time (three and a half years) during which a hostile king oppresses the holy ones. That language grew out of the persecution of the Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC; it was cleansed and rededicated in 164 BC, the origin of Hanukkah. Three and a half years, half of seven, became a standard figure for a limited time of distress. Revelation gives it as 42 months and 1,260 days, and it recurs in chapters 12 and 13.

Jesus warned that Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles were fulfilled (Luke 21:24). The Roman armies besieged the city in AD 70 and destroyed Herod's temple. If Revelation was written before AD 70, as some preterists hold, the measuring of the temple may refer to the historical temple; if written around AD 95, the temple had already been gone for a generation, and the image is almost certainly symbolic, as most interpreters take it anyway.
cultural:
Measuring was a prophetic sign of ownership and protection. Ezekiel saw an angel measure a future temple (Ezekiel 40 to 42), and Zechariah saw a man measure Jerusalem as a sign that God would dwell in it (Zechariah 2:1-5). The two witnesses are drawn from Zechariah 4, where two olive trees supply oil to a lampstand; there they stand for Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor, the two anointed ones. Their powers are those of Elijah, who shut the sky (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 both give the drought as three and a half years) and called down fire (2 Kings 1:10), and of Moses, who turned water to blood (Exodus 7:20). The law required two witnesses to establish testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Leaving bodies unburied was among the deepest dishonors in the ancient world (Psalm 79:2-3). Sending one another gifts was a way of celebrating a festival, as at Purim (Esther 9:19, 22), so the world keeps holiday over the prophets' deaths. The ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, disappeared when the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC; Jeremiah 3:16 foresaw a day when it would no longer be missed, and a later Jewish tradition preserved in 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 said Jeremiah had hidden it. Its appearance in heaven signals that God's covenant presence has never been lost.
literary: Verses 1 to 13 finish the interlude between the sixth and seventh trumpets, and verses 15 to 19 give the seventh trumpet itself, with verse 14 marking the second woe as past. The witnesses' story is told as a compressed gospel: ministry, rejection, death in the city where their Lord was crucified, public display, resurrection after three and a half days, and ascension in a cloud while their enemies watch. Verse 11 echoes Ezekiel 37, where the breath of life enters the dry bones. The seventh trumpet's hymn changes the divine title of 1:4 and 4:8: God is now “the One who is and who was”, with “is to come” dropped, because in the vision he has come and begun to reign. The chapter ends with the storm signs that closed the seals (8:5), lightning, rumblings, thunder, and earthquake, now with hail added, marking another ending in the book's spiral structure.

outline.t: The temple measured, the outer court given to the nations
The two witnesses and their power
The beast kills the witnesses and the world celebrates
The witnesses raised and taken up; the city shaken
The seventh trumpet: the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ
God's temple opened and the ark revealed

doctrines.note: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.” The kingdoms of this world are not merely defeated but taken over, one kingdom with one rightful king, as Daniel 7 and Psalm 2 foresaw.

The two witnesses, pictured as lampstands (the image Revelation uses for churches in 1:20), bear witness to the nations at the cost of their lives. Many read them as the church's calling in every age: prophetic testimony under pressure.

The elders praise God because the time has come to judge the dead, reward his servants, and “destroy those who destroy the earth.” Judgment is both reward and reckoning, and God's judgment falls on those who ruin what he made.

words.note: Martus, a witness, one who testifies to what they know. Revelation calls Jesus “the faithful witness” (1:5) and Antipas his faithful witness who was killed (2:13). By the second century the word was coming to mean a martyr, because witness to Christ so often led to death, and this chapter shows why.

Metreō, to measure. In prophecy, measuring marks what belongs to God and is under his protection, as in Ezekiel's and Zechariah's visions. The inner sanctuary and its worshipers are measured; the outer court is left exposed. God's people are kept safe in their relationship with him even while outwardly trampled.

Basileia, kingdom, rule, reign. The heart of Jesus' preaching was the kingdom of God (Mark 1:15). Here the word is singular: the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord. Revelation pictures not two kingdoms coexisting forever but one rule reclaimed.

Kibōtos, a chest or box, used for Noah's ark and for the ark of the covenant. The ark was the footstool of God's throne in Israel's sanctuary and the place of atonement. Seeing it in heaven's temple after centuries of absence assures readers that God's covenant stands.

christ: The two witnesses live out the story of Jesus. They testify, are killed in the city “where their Lord was also crucified,” lie dead for a short time, are raised by the breath of God, and ascend in a cloud, as Jesus did in Acts 1:9. Their story tells the church that faithful witness will follow the path of its Lord through death to vindication. The seventh trumpet then names Jesus directly: the kingdom now belongs to our Lord and to his Christ (Messiah, the anointed king). The joining of God and his Christ in one kingdom echoes Psalm 2, where the nations rage against the LORD and against his anointed, and where God sets his king on Zion. What the Psalm promised, the seventh trumpet announces as done.

hard.q: What are the temple and the two witnesses: literal or symbolic, past or future?
hard.a:
Each of the main schools reads them differently. Some preterists take the temple as the literal Jerusalem temple before its destruction in AD 70 and the forty-two months as the period of the Jewish war, with the two witnesses sometimes identified as Christian leaders of that era (some suggest Peter and Paul, both executed in Rome in the 60s by tradition). Futurists often expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem and two literal prophets in a final period of three and a half years; some early church writers identified them as Enoch and Elijah, who in Scripture did not die, and others expect Moses and Elijah, who appeared with Jesus at the Transfiguration. Historicists have matched the witnesses to faithful groups through church history. Idealists and many others read the temple as the people of God (as in 1 Corinthians 3:16 and Ephesians 2:21) and the two witnesses as the witnessing church, noting that they are called lampstands, the image for churches in 1:20, and that there are two because the law required two witnesses.

The great city is similarly debated: Jerusalem, where Jesus was crucified, or, since Revelation elsewhere calls Babylon the great city (16:19; 18:10), a figure for the whole world arrayed against God, called Sodom and Egypt to name its character. These are second-order questions. The chapter's direction is shared across the readings: faithful witness costs, and God vindicates.

questions: The witnesses' story follows the path of Jesus through death to resurrection. Where does faithfulness cost you something, and what hope does this chapter offer there?
The world celebrates when the prophets die because their message tormented them. Why do people often resent those who tell them the truth?
Heaven sings as if God's reign has already come. How might it change your week to live as though that verdict is already settled?
